problem: The stated reason is wrong. An ideal rectangular NRZ pulse of width T is 1 only for |t| < T/2 and is already 0 at t = ±T, ±2T, …, so it does satisfy p(nT) = 0 for n ≠ 0 at the sampling instants. It does not fail Nyquist's first criterion; it fails because its spectrum T·sinc(fT) has unbounded width, so no finite-bandwidth channel can pass it without spreading. The answer's claim that 'p(±T) is not zero and neighbours spill fully into each sample' contradicts the definition and will teach the wrong idea.
fix: Rewrite the question and answer: 'An ideal rectangular pulse of width T is zero at every other sampling instant, so it meets the zero-ISI condition on paper. Its spectrum is T·sinc(fT), which decays only as 1/f and is never zero, so undistorted transmission needs infinite bandwidth. Any real channel or filter of finite bandwidth rounds the edges, the pulse spreads past its T-second slot, and the tails land on the neighbouring samples as ISI.'

problem: The series names do not match the plotted data. The curve named a₋₁ p(t−T) peaks at t/T = 3 and the curve named a₀ p(t−2T) peaks at t/T = 4, but p(t−T) peaks at t/T = 1 and p(t−2T) peaks at t/T = 2. A student checking the labels against the axis will be confused.
fix: Either rename the series to a₋₁ p(t−3T) and a₀ p(t−4T), or shift the plotted functions so the peaks sit at t/T = 1 and t/T = 2, keeping the one-symbol-period spacing.

problem: The expression 'each contributes p(0.05T) plus p((k−n)T + 0.05T) terms' mixes up two things: p(0.05T) is the wanted pulse sampled slightly off its peak, not a neighbour's contribution. The final line 'peak distortion rises from 0' is also loose: for the untruncated sinc the timing-error ISI sum Σ δ/(n+δ) diverges, so in theory peak distortion becomes unbounded; only truncation keeps it finite in practice.
fix: Say: sampling at kT + 0.05T gives y = a_k p(0.05T) + Σ_{n≠k} a_n p((k−n)T + 0.05T). The neighbours' tails no longer sit at their zeros, so the ISI sum is nonzero even though it was exactly zero at the ideal instants. The wanted sample also drops slightly to p(0.05T). For an ideal sinc the timing-error ISI sum diverges; truncating the pulse keeps it finite but still large.
